Singapore industrial property prices up 4.2% y-o-y in third quarter; JTC notes 'good pipeline supply' of new space
article:
The industrial property market in Singapore showed continued resilience with sustained growth in both prices and rents in 3Q2026, alongside a “good pipeline supply” of new space coming up, JTC said in its latest quarterly market report.

In the third quarter, the price index for all industrial space islandwide continued its upward momentum and increased at a slightly quicker pace of 1.0% q-o-q and 4.2% y-o-y amid steady demand and low interest rates.

This is a tad faster than the previous quarter’s price growth of 0.6% q-o-q and 3.8% q-o-q.

Specifically, multiple-user factory spaces saw prices gain 1.1% q-o-q and 5.3% y-o-y, surpassing that of single-user factories, which logged increases of 0.8% q-o-q and 1.5% y-o-y.

Meanwhile, sale transaction volumes of all industrial properties were up by 8.1% y-o-y in the third quarter as compared to the year-ago period, going by caveats lodged.

Price index and number of transactions:

Tridiana Ong, head of occupier strategy and solutions at real estate consultancy Knight Frank Singapore, noted that total investment sales value climbed from an estimated $1.4 billion to about $2.0 billion, driven by a few large-ticket deals alongside sales from newly launched strata industrial developments.

In particular, although factories with remaining lease tenures of 30 years and below only saw a marginal increase in the number of transactions, their total sales value almost tripled from $360.7 million in the second quarter to $972.2 million.

“The increasing ticket sizes of some of these shorter-tenure factory assets, relative to the broader industrial market, underscored investor interest in industrial assets, particularly where value enhancement opportunities and competitive pricing can help offset leasehold constraints,” Ong said.

Another consultancy JLL foresees the JTC All Industrial Price Index to grow by about 3–4% for the full year.

This comes as “capital continues to seek shelter in safe havens like Singapore, driving further marginal yield compression”, said Chua Yang Liang, JLL’s head of research and consultancy for Southeast Asia.

Moderate rise in industrial rents

In the leasing market, the rental index for all industrial space edged up by 0.5% q-o-q and 2.1% y-o-y — mostly in line with inflation.

Rental index and number of transactions:

This stable rental growth trend, mirroring that of the previous quarter, is supported by global demand for semiconductors on the back of continual investment into AI, according to Chua from JLL.

“Asia Pacific economies including Southeast Asia countries like Singapore and Malaysia are firmly plugged into this growth driver,” he added.

The quarterly increase in leasing transactions for multi-user factories and warehouses was relatively measured.

That suggests that much of the demand stemmed from lease renewals and ongoing space requirements rather than expansionary moves, said Knight Frank’s Ong.

For business parks, rents kept steady even as the overall occupancy rate fell from 77.9% in the second quarter to 77.2% in the third quarter.

The JTC rental index for business parks stayed fairly stable with a 0.1% q-o-q uptick, after it had eased by 0.1% q-o-q in the previous quarter.

Business-park leasing activity grew 31.3% compared to the same quarter last year, rising from 80 contracts to 105.

“With office rents in the CBD remaining significantly higher and prime office supply constrained, business parks could offer possible space solutions, even though CBD locations remain favoured,” said Ong from Knight Frank.

Occupancy slips as users vacate older factories

The occupancy rate for all industrial space in Singapore eased slightly by 0.2 percentage point q-o-q in the third quarter to 88.9%.

JTC attributed the decrease to users vacating from older single-user and multi-user factories that have been earmarked for future redevelopment, as well as slower demand for suburban business parks.

On the other hand, the warehouse segment saw an increase of 0.3 percentage point in occupancy.

Changes in available stock, occupied stock and occupancy rate:

Chua of JLL pointed out that ongoing geopolitical tensions are weighing on occupier sentiment, with cost-cutting and space optimisation starting to impact overall occupancy levels.

That said, the underlying industrial demand remains firm. Singapore’s Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) increased slightly to 51.7 in September, from 51.5 in August, marking the 14th straight month of expansion above the 50-point threshold.

Companies that are rapidly expanding in pioneering industries “will increasingly be under pressure to consider other viable options like business parks or light industrial space as a cost-effective alternative to traditional CBD office locations”, said Ong from Knight Frank.

“This gradual broadening of occupier demand across locations and asset classes should enhance the market's overall resilience and support healthy leasing activity,” she continued.

Upcoming supply: single-user factories and warehouses

There remains a "good pipeline supply" of new industrial space, JTC noted on Oct 22.

Based on planning approvals as at end-September 2026, about 0.3 million sq m (about 3.23 million sq ft) of new industrial space is expected to be completed in the final quarter of this year.

Between 2027 and 2030, an average annual supply of 1.2 million sq m of industrial space is expected to be completed. That is higher than the average of about 1 million sq m of new completions over the past three years, JTC said.

In Knight Frank’s view, the industrial sector’s long-term prospects are positive, amid Singapore’s stable pro-business operating environment. This is even as growth is narrowing towards AI, advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries.

Despite Singapore’s largely leasehold industrial landscape, investor and owner-occupier interest remains firm.

“Capital continues to be directed towards industrial assets, with buyers increasingly prioritising properties that benefit from resilient occupier demand, dependable cash flows and opportunities to enhance value, rather than focusing solely on tenure,” Ong said.

Chua of JLL expects the uncertainty as well as elevated energy and freight costs from tensions in the Middle East to prompt businesses to adopt leaner operational models and delay expansion plans until there is greater clarity.

Nonetheless, JLL anticipates firm demand for high-specification premises, supported by order backlogs in the semiconductor sector, although near-term rental growth may be constrained by cost pressures and global disruptions.

title: Pair of adjoining freehold industrial properties in Jalan Senang Food Zone for sale at $18 mil
article:
A pair of adjoining freehold industrial properties in Jalan Senang’s approved Food Zone is being offered for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise, with a collective guide price of $18 million.

The two properties sit on a 9,017 sq ft land plot, translating to a price of around $1,996 psf, says marketing agent Huttons Asia.

Zoned for Business 1 use, the site has a plot ratio of 2.0 and an estimated maximum gross floor area of about 18,034 sq ft.

It also has a combined frontage measuring more than 30m and a depth of 27.5m, which provides good accessibility for loading and unloading, and operational flexibility, the firm adds.

Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics at Huttons Asia, said the properties’ existing cold storage capacity of up to 800 pallets gives incoming operators a head start by potentially saving them the time and capital required to fit out a new facility.

Located in District 14, Jalan Senang sits within an established light-industrial enclave in the Kembangan–Eunos area, where food-related businesses operate alongside other industrial uses.

Ong Jianlong, senior group district director at Huttons Asia, said the properties could appeal to food operators, cold-chain businesses, central kitchen operators and food manufacturers, as well as owner-occupiers looking for a sizeable freehold industrial property for their operations.

“Food operators usually have to settle for leasehold premises, where value declines as the lease runs down. It is rare to find two adjoining freehold food factories with a combined frontage of over 30m available for sale together,” he added.

The EOI exercise for the two properties will close on Oct 31 at 4pm.

title: Developer sale lifts The Arcady at Boon Keng to new price peak of $2,843 psf
article:
The Arcady at Boon Keng , a freehold condo in District 12, clinched first place among private non-landed residential developments that recorded fresh psf-price peaks during the week of Oct 6 to 13.

The project’s new benchmark of $2,843 psf was established on Oct 10, when a 678 sq ft, two-bedroom unit on the 22nd floor was sold by the developers for $1.93 million.

The sale inches past the project’s previous price high of $2,837 psf. That was set in November last year from the developer sale of a 764 sq ft two-bedder for $2.17 million.

The Arcady at Boon Keng is a 172-unit development along Saint Barnabas Lane, on the site of the former Euro-Asia Apartments . It offers one- to four-bedroom apartments ranging from 527 to 1,625 sq ft, as well as two penthouses measuring 2,433 and 2,583 sq ft.

Over its launch weekend in January 2024, the condo logged a 29.7% take-up rate at an average selling price of $2,570 psf. Based on caveats lodged as at Oct 20, the project is now 65.6% sold, with 59 apartments remaining.

The Arcady at Boon Keng is slated to receive its temporary occupation permit in 2027.

Second among the week’s top project highs was freehold condo Scotts 28 .

A 1,636 sq ft, three-bedroom unit notched a new record of $2,511 psf for the development when it fetched $4.11 million on Oct 9.

That is the first time a unit at Scotts 28 has transacted above the $2,500 psf threshold, surpassing the previous peak of $2,481 psf. That was in May 2023 when a 1,733 sq ft three-bedder was sold for $4.3 million.

The 136-unit Scotts 28 is located just off Orchard Road, next to Goodwood Park Hotel, in prime District 9. Completed in 1998, it comprises two- to five-bedroom units ranging from 1,098 to 4,650 sq ft.

Shopping malls such as Far East Plaza , Scotts Square and Tang Plaza are within a 10-minute walk. The Newton MRT interchange is about five minutes away on foot.

The highest absolute quantum recorded at the condo thus far was from the sub-sale of a 3,466 sq ft three-bedder for $6.86 million ($1,979 psf) in 1996.

Meanwhile, Caribbean At Keppel Bay rounded out the top three psf-price highs for the week.

A 2,390 sq ft, four-bedroom unit on the third floor scored a fresh record of $2,339 psf when it changed hands for $5.59 million on Oct 13.

Completed in 2004, Caribbean At Keppel Bay has 969 units housed in 12 residential blocks. Its one- to five-bedroom units range from 893 to 4,650 sq ft.

The 99-year leasehold condo, situated along Keppel Bay Drive in District 4, is within a 10-minute walk to Harbourfront MRT interchange.

Based on caveats compiled by EdgeProp Singapore , resale prices at the condo have averaged $1,924 psf over the past 12 months.

Also logging a psf-price high during the period in review was City Square Residences on Kitchener Link.

A three-bedroom apartment at the freehold condo was transacted at $2,294 psf or nearly $2.84 million on Oct 12, putting it in fourth place among the week’s top project highs. Measuring 1,238 sq ft, the unit sits on the 17th floor.

This is a tad higher than the previous benchmark of $2,278 psf at City Square Residences. That earlier record was set in March 2025 when a larger three-bedder, spanning 1,496 sq ft, was resold for about $3.41 million.

The condo is right across the road from City Square Mall , which has a basement connection to Farrer Park MRT Station, and a three-minute walk to the 24-hour Mustafa Centre .

There were no new psf-price lows for the week.

title: Four-bedder at Caribbean At Keppel Bay sold for $3.3 mil profit
article:
The sale of a four-bedroom apartment at Caribbean At Keppel Bay , a 99-year leasehold development in District 4, was the most profitable condo resale deal during the week of Oct 6 to 13.

The seller of the 2,390 sq ft unit on the third floor reaped a $3.34 million (148.5%) gain when it changed hands for about $5.59 million ($2,339 psf) on Oct 13. The seller had bought the unit from the developer for $2.25 million ($941 psf) in October 2000.

This works out to an annualised profit of 3.6% over a holding period of 26 years.

The transaction sets a new record profit for resale deals at the development. It surpasses the previous top gain of $2.71 million, which came from the sale of another four-bedder last December.

That 2,433 sq ft unit, which was previously purchased for around $2.3 million in October 2000, was subsequently sold for $5 million on Dec 16, 2025.

Caribbean At Keppel Bay is a 969-unit development completed in 2004. Located on Keppel Bay Drive, the waterfront development comprises 23 residential blocks, each rising 10 storeys.

Units at the condo start from two-bedders of 840 sq ft and go up to four-bedders of 3,541 sq ft. There are also penthouses measuring 4,650 to 6,135 sq ft.

The development is close to HarbourFront MRT Station (an interchange for the Circle and North-East lines) and retail mall VivoCity . Lifestyle and recreational facilities at Sentosa Cove are also nearby.

Apart from the Oct 13 transaction, Caribbean At Keppel Bay has logged 28 other resale transactions this year. Caveats tabulated by EdgeProp Singapore show that 27 of these were in the black, with owners netting gains ranging from $95,000 to $1.46 million.

The second-highest profit for the week came from a unit at Grange Residences , a District 10 development. The 2,852 sq ft, four-bedroom apartment was sold for $10.2 million on Oct 12, with the seller netting a $2.9 million (39.7%) surplus.

The figure translates to a 3% annualised gain over a holding period of around 11.5 years. The unit was previously transacted for $7.3 million in May 2015.

The deal is far from the most profitable transaction at Grange Residences. The record profit stands at $6.5 million, achieved from the sale of another four-bedroom unit in June 2025.

That 2,852 sq ft unit fetched $9.85 million, after the owner had purchased it for $3.35 million in June 2004. As a result, the owner made an annualised gain of 5.3% over 21 years.

Completed in 2004, Grange Residences is a freehold development on Grange Road in District 10. Featuring three 18-storey blocks, it has 164 residences in four-bedroom layouts of 2,486 to 2,852 sq ft.

The condo is close to Tanglin Mall and the Orchard Road shopping belt.

On the other end of the spectrum , Marina Collection in Sentosa Cove saw the steepest loss for the week.

A four-bedroom unit measuring 2,185 sq ft was sold for $3.1 million ($1,419 psf) on Oct 9, leaving the seller $2.36 million in the red.

The unit was purchased for $5.46 million ($2,500 psf) in February 2010. As such, the sale resulted in a loss of 43.3%, or 3.3% annualised over more than 16 years.

Though the seller incurred a seven-digit deficit, it is still significantly less than the $5.87 million loss booked on a five-bedroom unit last month, which set a new record low for Marina Collection.

The 4,725 sq ft apartment fetched $6.8 million on Sept 3. The seller, who bought the fourth-floor unit for $12.67 million in January 2008, suffered a 46.3% loss, or 3.3% annualised over nearly 19 years.

Marina Collection is a 99-year leasehold condo completed in 2011. It has 124 units across three four-storey blocks, with three- to five-bedders of 1,873 to 4,725 sq ft.

The development is a 10-minute walk from Quayside Isle , a mixed-use development along the Sentosa Cove waterfront with shops and eateries. VivoCity is an eight-minute drive away.

title: Rare five-bedroom penthouse at Grandeur Park Residences to go on auction at $3.18 mil
article:
A penthouse at Grandeur Park Residences , a 99-year leasehold condo in District 16, will be put up for auction by SRI on Oct 28. The 1,744 sq ft five-bedder has a guide price of $3.18 million, which translates to $1,823 psf.

Offered via an owner’s sale, this is the first time the property will go under the hammer.

Caveats lodged show that the unit was previously purchased from the developer for $2.03 million ($1,164 psf) in March 2017.

The unit is one of only three five-bedroom penthouses at Grandeur Park Residences. Occupying the top floor of one of the development’s six towers, thethree penthouses are the condo’s largest units.

The 14th-floor residence is served by a private lift and features a combined living and dining area that opens out to a balcony. The unit also has a master bedroom with an en suite bathroom; wet and dry kitchens; and four common bedrooms, one of which features a loft accessed by a staircase.

Mok Sze Sze, managing partner of SRI Auction, says the unit was renovated about five years ago, when the owners moved in, and has been well-maintained.

High ceilings across most of the living spaces also make the residence appealing to prospective buyers seeking a spacious home, she adds.

Located on Bedok South Avenue 3, Grandeur Park Residences is a 720-unit condo that was completed in 2020. It features one- to five-bedroom units ranging from 420 to 1,744 sq ft.

It is a five-minute walk from Tanah Merah MRT Station, while retail and lifestyle amenities at Bedok Mall, Eastpoint Mall and Changi City Point are within a four- to nine-minute drive.

Grandeur Park Residences has seen a relatively high volume of resale transactions this year, recording a total of 28 thus far.

Based on URA caveats, the most recent resale transaction involved a 452 sq ft, one-bedroom unit on the third floor, which changed hands for $860,000 ($1,902 psf) on Oct 9.

Before that, two units at Grandeur Park Residences were sold on Oct 1: a 420 sq ft one-bedder for $820,000 ($1,953 psf), and a 1,130 sq ft four-bedder for $2.38 million ($2,106 psf).

The last time a five-bedroom penthouse changed hands at the development was in November 2025. That unit, also measuring 1,744 sq ft, fetched around $2.82 million, or $1,616 psf.

title: Hong Kong's primary residential market sees wave of launches
article:
Hong Kong homebuyers are poised to see new residential launches in the coming days and weeks following a sell-out weekend of more than 360 flats in two major projects in the city.

Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHKP), one of Hong Kong’s major developers and landlords, was set to hold a second round of sales for Sierra Sea Phase 2C(2) in Shap Sze Heung, which is between Sai Kung and Ma On Shan, with 152 flats on offer as at Oct 14, it said in a statement.

Among them, 128 flats would be sold via a regular price list and the remaining 24 flats would be offered for sale via tender.

The new batch would include flats with layouts of two bedrooms and three bedrooms and saleable areas of 418 to 679 sq ft. The flats to be offered via a price list would be sold at discounted rates starting from HK$12,714 ($2,070) psf, or a per-flat price of about HK$5.47 million to about HK$9.87 million.

The latest round of sales comes after SHKP sold all 142 flats on offer in the same project on Oct 17. These flats also had sizes ranging from 418 to 679 sq ft with discounted prices from HK$5.38 million.

Yuexiu Property also sold out on the same day all the 220 flats it put on offer via a price list at The Atlas Phase 1 project in Yau Tong. The flats comprised layouts with one to two bedrooms measuring 285 to 510 sq ft.

Yuexiu announced that 132 flats would be on offer via regular sale on Oct 24. The flats would range in sizes of between 278 and 497 sq ft. The discounted psf-price would start at HK$13,038 to HK$16,769.

“Primary launches continue to clearly outperform the secondary market,” said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties. “Developers maintain the upper hand by offering aggressive price cuts, flexible payment schemes and attractive rebates to drive swift inventory turnover.”

CK Asset Holdings, the flagship property developer of billionaire Li Ka-shing and family, is also set to commence the soft marketing for its Montage residential development in Kam Tin North.

The development provides 327 homes, including multi-storey layouts with one to two bedrooms as well as houses with two to four bedrooms.

The anticipated flurry of sales comes after the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate in September while major Hong Kong banks have so far held rates steady. The market generally expected the Fed to hold rates in October, but another increase is possible by the end of the year.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority moves in lockstep with the Fed to keep the local currency’s peg to the US dollar. Higher interest rates could lead to higher mortgage payments by those seeking loans to buy property.

“Given the expectation of an interest rate hike, developers are likely to adopt a distinctly ‘volume-led, price-capped’ pricing strategy to maintain a healthy leverage position,” said Norry Lee, senior director of projects strategy and consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong.

Beyond the residential segment, Hong Kong’s office property received a boost with Swire Properties and Chinachem Group announcing plans to redevelop Sea View Building and Hoi Wan Building, together with the adjoining Chinachem Exchange Square, into a premium Grade A harbourfront office tower in Taikoo Place.

The combined site spans around 35,000 sq ft, enabling a larger, integrated commercial development. The project is expected to deliver about 500,000 sq ft of gross floor area, comprising a 27-storey office tower, a retail podium and basement car parking facilities. The new development is expected to break ground in 2027.

The planned office tower forms part of Swire Properties’ ongoing expansion of Taikoo Place under its HK$100 billion investment plan, while also advancing Chinachem Group’s commitment to enhance and optimise its portfolio over the long term.

The redevelopment is taking place amid a gradual recovery in the city’s office property sector.

Hong Kong’s overall prime office market saw its vacancy rate drop to 12.5% in August from 13.5% a year earlier, according to Morgan Stanley. Central led the recovery, with rents rising 7.3% as vacancy declined to 7.8% from 11.2%.

title: Causeway Point AEI to introduce new social and reading hub with pre-loved books, Sing Lit
article:
A new first-of-its-kind public "social and reading destination", repurposed from a cinema, will be one of the highlights of Causeway Point ’s upcoming transformation.

As part of the Woodlands mall's extensive asset enhancement initiative (AEI) — slated to start in the second quarter of 2027 and complete by the end of 2029 — the space is expected to open in 2028.

Named The HomePage @ Causeway Point, it is intended to bring together reading, literary experiences and community programmes for visitors of all ages, said Frasers Centrepoint Trust (FCT) and the National Library & Archives Board (NLB) in a joint statement on Oct 22.

The HomePage will span more than 32,000 sq ft across a triple-volume space on parts of the mall's sixth and seventh floors.

FCT and NLB have inked an MOU to collaborate on the planning, design and implementation, including its literary collections, community programmes and visitor experiences.

It will house one of Singapore’s largest publicly accessible collections of pre-loved books from NLB’s libraries in English and Mother Tongue languages, as well as one of the country’s most extensive showcases of Singapore literature (Sing Lit) and local authors.

Visitors can browse and take home the pre-loved books without borrowing them, allowing them to explore titles at their own pace.

They are also encouraged to share books they have enjoyed with others, so that more members of the community can benefit from the collection.

Meanwhile, the dedicated Sing Lit showcase will feature a diverse selection of titles, as well as thematic exhibitions and programmes. NLB will also collaborate with the National Arts Council to curate the Sing Lit space.

Social hub with books, play zones and theatre

Designed as a social hub, The HomePage will also feature interactive experiences and family-friendly amenities such as children’s play zones. Visitors can consume F&B within the community reading space as well.

A purpose-built indoor theatre and screening space within will host film screenings, author talks, storytelling sessions and cultural programmes.

"Whether visitors are reading, enjoying a meal, attending a film screening or spending time with family and friends, we want this to be a place where people feel welcome to stay, connect and return to," said Richard Ng, CEO of FCT’s manager.

He added that FCT is working with NLB to showcase archives of old movies. There will also be "a lot of potential" to continuously curate new activities and programming, especially at The Social Steps, which is designed as a terraced public living room.

Moreover, The HomePage will serve as a starting point for more people to discover books and the joy of reading and build a lifelong reading habit.

Melissa Tam, CEO of NLB, said: "By making reading more accessible and creating new opportunities for readers to discover Sing Lit and local authors, we hope to encourage more Singaporeans to embrace reading as a lifelong habit and connect more deeply with our shared heritage and identity."

New tenant mix and community spaces after revamp

Through Causeway Point's upcoming AEI, the Reit aims to reposition the mall as a regional destination offering a wider range of retail, dining, lifestyle and community experiences.

The total cost of the AEI has yet to be finalised, pending the outcome of the tender process. FCT expects to be able to share the figure sometime in early 2027, Ng said.

The enhanced mall, spanning over 425,000 sq ft, will have a rebalanced tenant mix with close to 250 stores offering everyday essentials, unique fashion, healthcare, beauty and experiential dining concepts.

There will also be new community spaces, family-friendly amenities and upgraded facilities, while each level of the mall will be curated into a distinct lifestyle zone.

In late July, Metro had said it would downsize its premises at both Causeway Point and Paragon by closing its existing large-format department stores when the leases conclude, and instead shift towards more flexible multi-concept stores.

Metro is currently the anchor tenant at Causeway Point, occupying about 54,000 sq ft.

At the MOU signing event on Oct 20, Ng confirmed that FCT is still in discussions with Metro on next steps. "They have talked about potentially doing a modular concept… They would like to stay on and we do see the value they bring… It’s about getting the right concept that works for our newly revamped Causeway Point," he added.

The mall's AEI comes as northern Singapore continues to grow as a major residential and commercial hub, supported by sustained population growth and the planned addition of more than 50,000 new homes.

First opened in 1998, Causeway Point has been welcoming over 27 million shoppers annually in recent years.

Its location within the Woodlands Regional Centre, direct connectivity to the Woodlands MRT and bus interchanges and proximity to the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link makes it well-positioned to serve a growing northern region, Ng said.

"Yet as we know, every successful mall needs to evolve over time," he added. To stay ahead and capture the growth opportunities in the northern region of Singapore, the Reit aims to transform Causeway Point into a leading regional mall.

DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) has delivered a total return of 37%.
Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd
(SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, has returned 26.1%, and
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68), or SGX, 24.3%.
The three have something else in common.
Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, owned 28% of DBS and 51% of ST Engineering as at 31 March 2026.
It also held 23.35% of SGX through SEL Holdings as at 1 September 2026.
Is Temasek the secret ingredient? Probably not.
In a 2011 letter, Temasek said it plays no part in SGX’s governance or operations, and that the law bars SEL Holdings from voting its SGX shares.
The better answer lies in the businesses themselves.
Can SGX keep raising its dividend if trading cools?
For its fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), SGX grew net revenue by 13.9% year on year (YoY) to S$1.5 billion.
Equities – Cash revenue rose 28.1% to S$502.9 million as securities daily average traded value climbed 34.9% to S$1.8 billion.
Reported net profit rose a more modest 7.8% to S$698.4 million.
A S$53.4 million goodwill impairment on Scientific Beta and weaker investment gains weighed on the figure.
Strip those out, and adjusted net profit grew 24.6% to S$759.5 million.
SGX has proposed an ordinary dividend of S$0.445 per share for FY2026, plus a one-off dividend of S$0.125.
That brings the total to S$0.570, compared with S$0.375 for FY2025.
The bourse operator held S$1.8 billion of cash against S$628.2 million of borrowings, and it plans to repay all its debt in FY2027.
Management has also guided for quarterly dividend increases of 0.25 cents through FY2028. Investors may be paying up for that visibility.
Here’s the thing: SGX earns more when markets are busy.
A long lull in trading would test its medium-term target of 6% to 8% revenue growth, excluding treasury income.

How is DBS growing profit while interest rates fall?
Falling rates tend to squeeze banks, and DBS felt it.
For the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026), net interest income slipped 2% YoY to S$3.6 billion.
The net interest margin (NIM) narrowed to 1.87% from 2.05%.
Total income still rose 6% to S$6.1 billion, crossing S$6 billion for the first time.
How?
Non-interest income rose about 21% to S$2.5 billion, with wealth management fees up 42% to S$919 million.
Net profit climbed 9% to S$3.1 billion, for a return on equity of 17.9%.
The non-performing loan ratio held steady at 1.0%.
In other words, investors may be rewarding a bank that depends less on interest rates.
For 2Q2026, the board declared an interim dividend of S$0.66 per share.
It also declared a separate capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share, bringing the quarter’s total to S$0.81.
Management has raised its full-year guidance and expects 2026 total income to exceed 2025’s level.
The risk? Margins could come under more pressure if rates keep falling.

Can ST Engineering’s order book fund a rising dividend?
ST Engineering’s operating profit is growing faster than its sales in all three segments.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 11.1% YoY to S$6.6 billion, while net profit climbed 27.1% to S$512.1 million.
Commercial Aerospace and Urban Solutions & Satcom each grew revenue by 15%.
Rail and tolling deliveries lifted the latter’s operating profit fourfold.
Cash generation kept pace.
Free cash flow rose 22.1% to S$591.6 million.
Shareholders received S$0.09 per share for the half, up from S$0.08 a year ago, and the group plans another S$0.05 for 3Q2026.
The order book hit a record S$35.7 billion.
About S$5.7 billion of that is due for delivery over the rest of 2026.
Investors may be pricing in that visibility.
Watch the balance sheet. Cash fell to S$255.3 million at 30 June 2026, from S$576.4 million at end-2025.
Borrowings, which include lease liabilities, eased to S$4.7 billion from S$4.8 billion.
Free cash flow is what fuels dividends, and ST Engineering needs it to keep growing to cover its debt and a rising payout.

So why bother with

at all?
Because a good business can grow its payout over time.

Does Info-Tech have the cash to back its dividend?
Info-Tech Systems Ltd.
(SGX: ITS) sells cloud-based human resource, accounting and customer relationship software.
It listed on the SGX Mainboard in July 2025.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 22% year on year (YoY) to S$27.3 million.
Subscriptions brought in S$21.2 million, up 12%, while services revenue more than doubled to S$4.9 million on demand for AI training.
Profit rose 89% to S$9.7 million.
Look closer, and two one-offs flatter that growth.
This year included a S$1.0 million Enterprise Singapore grant, while last year carried about S$2.0 million in listing expenses.
Strip both out, and adjusted profit after tax rose a more measured 20% to S$8.7 million.
Here’s where Info-Tech shines.
The board raised its interim dividend to S$0.0168 per share from S$0.0155.
That payout costs S$4.3 million, less than half of net profit.
Free cash flow more than doubled to S$15.1 million, over three times the dividend payout.
The group held S$76.6 million in cash with no borrowings.
Here’s the thing: S$6.9 million of that free cash flow came from customers paying what they owed.
That boost may not repeat.
Info-Tech also has only a short record as a listed dividend payer.

Can VICOM’s bigger dividend outlast ERP 2.0?
VICOM Ltd
(SGX: WJP), a subsidiary of
ComfortDelGro Corporation Limited
(SGX: C52), carries out Singapore’s mandatory vehicle inspections.
In 1H2026, revenue grew 6.4% YoY to S$74.3 million.
Total operating costs fell 1.2% to S$50.3 million as subcontractor fees on the ERP 2.0 On-Board Unit project dropped 44.2%.
With revenue up and costs down, profit attributable to shareholders rose 28% to S$19.9 million.
VICOM’s interim dividend rose 27.4% to S$0.0395 per share, about 70% of earnings per share of S$0.0561.
Cash flow kept pace.
Operating cash flow grew 65.1% to S$31.8 million, and free cash flow more than doubled to S$14.7 million even after S$17.2 million of capital expenditure.
VICOM held S$53 million in cash, with no bank borrowings.
So what’s the catch?
The On-Board Unit project wraps up in December 2026, and management expects a softer second half.
Interest income halved to S$0.4 million as rates fell, while the Middle East conflict clouds demand for Oil & Gas testing.
And because VICOM pays out a larger share of its profit than Info-Tech, it has less room to absorb a dip.

Can QAF’s balance sheet carry the dividend through a restructuring?
QAF Limited
(SGX: Q01) bakes bread under brands such as Gardenia, while its Ben Foods Group arm imports and distributes food and beverages.
On the surface, 1H2026 looked steady.
Revenue was flat at S$306.7 million, up 0.2% YoY; it would have grown 2% in constant currency.
Operating profit rose 87% to S$15.3 million.
A S$4.3 million foreign currency gain helped, as did cuts of 15% in utilities costs and 36% in advertising spend.
The bottom line tells a different story.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 51% to S$1.9 million.
QAF booked S$10 million of exceptional costs as it closes its Singapore manufacturing facilities, and took a S$3.9 million non-cash impairment on its Malaysian joint venture.
Exclude both, and profit before tax came to S$16.5 million, though that still includes the currency gain.
Free cash flow more than halved to S$5.3 million, yet QAF kept its interim dividend unchanged at S$0.01 per share.
How can it afford that?
Look at its balance sheet.
QAF held S$204.8 million in cash against just S$6.5 million of debt, excluding lease liabilities.
That net cash position buys the company time.
Time alone isn’t a business plan, though.
Management flagged ongoing cost pressures and unpredictable currency moves, and expects further transition costs will follow as bakery production shifts to Malaysia.
Until earnings recover, this dividend leans more on QAF’s savings than on its earnings.

Portfolio occupancy eased to 96.4% in 1Q FY2027, from 96.9% in the previous quarter.
Occupancy fell in Singapore, China, and Australia because of leasing downtime.
Blended portfolio rental reversion was +0.9%, or +2.3% excluding China.
Outside China, every market that reported a reversion figure was positive this quarter.
China remains MLT’s weakest market, but its rental reversions have improved steadily for seven straight quarters and are on the verge of reaching zero.
China’s reversion should turn positive within the next few quarters, but the final stretch looks to be the slowest.
China’s occupancy slipped to 93.8% from 94.2%.
The manager noted that this still compares favourably with the Chinese logistics industry average of around 80%.
Why lease expiries matter for distributions
MLT’s weighted average lease expiry (WALE) stood at 2.5 years, down from 2.7 years a year ago.
More than half its leases expire in FY2027 and FY2028 — an area to watch.
The balance sheet is stable, with one soft spot.
MLT’s debt metrics are broadly unchanged from a year ago:
Gearing: 40.5% (41.2% a year ago)
Cost of debt: 2.6% (2.7%)
Fixed-rate debt: 82% (84%)
Interest cover ratio: 2.9 times (2.9 times)
A lower cost of debt and a high share of fixed-rate borrowings help protect distributions from rate swings.
The interest cover ratio is the soft spot.
At 2.9 times, it clears the regulatory requirement.
But it leaves a thin buffer if borrowing costs stay high.
Related articles:

The Logistics Boom: Why Mapletree Logistics Trust Is a Global Powerhouse
A new exit route out of China
Hong Kong SAR and China together still account for around 41% of MLT’s assets under management and roughly 31% of gross revenue.
After the quarter closed, MLT announced three divestments with a total agreed property value of around S$155 million, namely Mapletree (Wuxi) Logistics Park, Mapletree Wuxi New District Logistics Park, and 39 Changi South Avenue 2 in Singapore.
The two Wuxi properties form part of the seed portfolio of the Mapletree China Logistics RMB Fund.
The fund was launched by MLT’s sponsor, Mapletree Investments, with China Life Capital, and is valued at around RMB1.5 billion.
The two Wuxi sales are not a material change on their own.
What has changed is that a route out now exists.
If the sponsor scales up the fund, MLT gains a way to exit Chinese assets without relying on third-party buyers.
For the record, as of 15 July 2026, MLT had completed S$300 million of divestments out of a pipeline of about S$1 billion identified in FY2025.
The manager’s
outlook is cautious
.
It expects the global economy to moderate on high energy prices and persistent inflation.
It also sees currency volatility and elevated borrowing costs continuing as headwinds.
On the positive side, leasing demand is holding up.
Get Smart: a solid yield, but growth is still missing

There are several positives that support the REIT’s distribution: occupancy above 96%, positive rental reversions outside China, mostly fixed-rate debt, and the first year-on-year DPU increase since 3Q FY2024.
But the recent DPU gain came mainly from lower costs, not rising income.
For the distribution to keep growing, two things need to happen: China’s rental reversions need to turn positive, and the manager needs to keep using its sponsor’s fund to recycle capital.
Until China’s rental reversions turn positive and divestment proceeds are redeployed into income-producing assets, headwinds are likely to keep any improvement in MLT’s distributions subdued.

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs in AI-fuelled push to lower costs
article:
LONDON (Oct 22): Barclays Plc said it’s cutting 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of total headcount, as part of a “technology-enabled” effort to reduce costs as it adopts artificial intelligence across the bank.

The bank reported third-quarter earnings Thursday that missed several key estimates. Barclays’ bond traders suffered the biggest slump on Wall Street during the quarter, taking the shine off a strong performance on the equities desk.

Revenue from fixed income and currency trading fell 19% compared with a year earlier to £1.01 billion (US$1.4 billion or $1.8 billion), behind analyst expectations compiled by Bloomberg. That meant the equities traders, who posted a 47% jump in revenue, almost matched that revenue haul with their best performance since at least 2009, the year after Barclays acquired the North American business of Lehman Brothers.

The bank said the fixed-income result reflected lower client activity in rates and credit, and “further adversity in September due to the macroeconomic environment.” On a call with reporters, chief executive officer CS Venkatakrishnan said the performance in FICC was “somewhat disappointing.”

“We will employ AI at scale,” Venkatakrishnan said on the call. “But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake.”

Barclays cut about 1,000 jobs in the first six months of this year, with the remaining due before the end of 2026. About 60% of the job cuts are coming within support functions, including among developers. Barclays employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025.

See also: Westpac axes 140 more roles as Australia bank job cuts intensify

The London-based bank said it was “structurally reducing” costs to “generate capacity for investment.” It’s focusing on simplifying the organisation and increasing efficiency, driven by AI, according to a presentation.

Shares in Barclays were trading as much as 2.4% lower as the London market opened.

The bank cut £201 million of costs in the three months through September, and plans to cut about £300 million more in the final quarter of the year.

See also: HDFC Bank probe finds that senior executives leaked secrets — Bloomberg

Barclays’ retail bank couldn’t do enough to overcome weakness in the investment bank, with the UK retail unit broadly stable and the US consumer arm also roughly flat year on year, missing estimates.

The bank stuck to its targets for the coming years, with operating expenses largely as expected in the quarter, and announced a £500 million share buyback. Investors have been watching the bank’s cost control after it reported disappointingly high expenses in its half-year earnings, despite a fresh cost-cutting programme announced in February.

Peers including JPMorgan Chase & Co, Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Bank of America Corp saw similar trends across fixed income desks, where revenue fell as much as 17% year-on-year as they dealt with the impact of rising interest rates, which can push down the value of existing debt and crimp demand from clients to transact.

Overall the Barclays investment bank slightly missed expectations with total income of £3.13 billion.

“With one quarter to go before the end of our original three-year plan, we have either achieved or are on track to achieve all of our 2026 group targets. We are confident in and committed to the 2028 targets that we laid out earlier in the year,” Venkatakrishnan said in a statement.

UK lenders are bracing for a rise in taxes on their earnings as part of the Labour government’s budget next week, which would use the proceeds to fund cost-of-living relief for households.

title: Evergrande liquidators plan first payout to creditors next year
article:
(Oct 22): Nearly three years after China Evergrande Group began winding up, liquidators have recovered less than 1% of the US$46 billion sought by creditors, which they aim to begin distributing in the first half of 2027.

Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong, from the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal Inc, said on Thursday that they’ve raised about HK$3.4 billion (US$433 million) as of Sept 30. For the first time, the court-appointed liquidators published a detailed breakdown of how much they recouped from various assets, including aircraft, artwork and club memberships.

Evergrande’s dramatic collapse has become an emblem of the prolonged Chinese property crisis that’s still rippling through the world’s second-biggest economy. The company’s creditors have faced multiple twists and turns in their quest to recover their money, including the August sentencing of Evergrande’s founder Hui Ka Yan to life in prison.

The liquidators on Thursday gave their second progress report since they set out on the monumental task of sifting through Evergrande’s web of holdings across the globe. The company had 3,000 legal entities in multiple jurisdictions, as well as about 1,300 projects under development in more than 280 cities.

Middleton and Wong said they’re still adjudicating 200 debt claims and didn’t say how much creditors should expect to receive in their first payment. In 2023, Deloitte estimated that the recovery rate for the company’s dollar notes would be 3.4% on average if the firm was liquidated.

See also: Barclays’ Middle East expansion plans ‘on track,’ Khanna says

The liquidators said they’ve entered exclusive talks to sell a majority stake in Evergrande’s property management unit, one of three large potential sources of cash. Asian private equity firm PAG was in discussions to buy the stake, Bloomberg reported earlier, after negotiations with a Chinese state-owned suitor broke down.

But the liquidators also stressed that severe challenges remain because many of Evergrande’s assets have been difficult to sell.

For example, an Airbus A319 jet is still parked at an airport in Guangzhou and hasn’t been airworthy since 2023, they said. A buyer has signed an agreement that should generate about US$12 million after an initial deal fell through.

See also: Citi targets top spot in China as it awaits securities licence

The liquidators also managed to raise HK$255 million by disposing of artwork including some by Picasso and Monet, though the pieces were sold at a loss. The paintings were “hurriedly and improperly” moved to a storeroom in Evergrande’s headquarters, and didn’t appear to have been packaged properly, they said.

The liquidators said there’s only a “remote” chance they’ll be able to recover assets held by Evergrande’s subsidiaries in mainland China, where the company was once the biggest property developer by sales. They haven’t been granted direct access to Chinese information systems. While a large amount of documentation has been found, much of it is fragmented and incomplete.

More than 650 of Evergrande’s entities have entered bankruptcy administration in mainland China. The company’s Guangzhou Kailong Real Estate unit, which holds a roughly 60% stake in Evergrande’s primary onshore property development arm, has received claims from the liquidators for about HK$1.4 billion of debt.

Middleton and Wong have launched a series of lawsuits to aid their pursuit of Evergrande’s funds.

They are trying to claw back US$6.5 billion in dividends and remuneration from former executives including Hui, Ex-chief executive officer Xia Haijun and Hui’s ex-wife Ding Yumei.

In one of the largest corporate claims ever filed in Hong Kong, the liquidators are also targeting a total of 57 billion yuan (US$8.5 billion) from PricewaterhouseCoopers International Ltd and its affiliates in mainland China and Hong Kong.

The liquidators have also brought Hong Kong’s regulator to court, seeking to void a HK$1 billion fund that PwC’s Hong Kong affiliate agreed to establish to compensate shareholders. The Securities and Futures Commission struck the settlement deal in April following investigations into the firm’s auditing work for Evergrande. A judgement is expected to come before the end of October.

title: SoftBank's market value halves from peak as AI fears grow
article:
(Oct 22): SoftBank Group Corp’s market value halved from its peak in June, as higher borrowing costs fuel investor concerns over the sustainability of its massive investments in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares of the Tokyo-based company fell 6.9% on Thursday, taking their drop from an all-time high struck on June 2 to 50%, with earnings from US megacaps failing to ease the angst. After briefly overtaking Toyota Motor Corp as Japan’s biggest company four months ago, its market capitalisation is now about ¥24.7 trillion (US$157 billion or $201 billion), smaller than that of Hitachi Ltd and Recruit Holdings Co.

Global concerns over AI spending had accelerated after US-based cloud-computing provider CoreWeave Inc’s bonds fell to levels associated with distress, exposing financing risks across the industry.

“SoftBank’s vulnerability stands out as investors increasingly scrutinise the financial health of AI-related companies, given the group’s highly leveraged financial structure and growing borrowing costs,” said Kazuyuki Muramatsu, the head of investment management at Nagomi Capital. If global sentiment towards the AI growth story turns sour, it may lead to valuation losses for SoftBank’s Vision Fund, which would in turn result in higher premium for future funding, he said.

The price to insure SoftBank’s debt against default has climbed, with credit-default swaps rising to the highest level in nearly four years on Tuesday. With the company relying on debt financing for much of its investments across the AI ecosystem, ranging from infrastructure and energy to robotics, CoreWeave’s troubles dented confidence even in equity investors who had earlier focused on returns from SoftBank’s AI bets. The stock is Nikkei’s worst performer so far this month, down more than 30% and wiping out all gains from September.

See also: Red Hat opens Apac AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore, signs DSTA pact

Rising competition among AI models also remains an overhang. OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested almost US$65 billion, now faces more affordable Chinese rivals offering comparable performance.

SoftBank raised US$11.1 billion in September via the largest corporate junk bond sale on record to finance founder Masayoshi Son’s big AI ambitions.

title: Bitcoin falls below US$83,000 as AI jitters weigh on sentiment
article:
(Oct 22): Bitcoin retreated below US$83,000 ($105,980) Thursday, giving up the previous session’s gains even as investors returned to US spot exchange-traded funds.

The original cryptocurrency fell as much as 2.4% in early Asia trading, standing around US$82,700 as of 1pm in Singapore. Smaller tokens ether, solana and XRP also saw falls of roughly 2% to 3.5%.

The retreat coincided with renewed pressure on risk assets as investors weighed mixed technology earnings and escalating Middle East tensions that have pushed oil prices higher. Asia equities and US stock futures were down, while Brent crude climbed above US$110.

Weakness in equities has pushed bitcoin “back to its recent range,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. “We expect US$85,000 to be retested again in the coming days, though conviction is likely to stay limited,” she added, noting that hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve could weigh on sentiment.

Institutional demand for bitcoin looked to be returning in recent days with strong ETF inflows. US-listed spot bitcoin ETFs have seen US$1.1 billion in net inflows so far this week, recovering from the US$909.6 million in outflows from the previous two weeks.

Options pricing on Deribit still shows a preference for downside protection. The largest outstanding positions for options to sell bitcoin expiring Friday were at a strike price of US$78,000.

See also: JPMorgan brings deposit token to ethereum for institutional clients

Bitcoin is down by a third from its all-time high above US$126,000 a year ago. A rebound since August raised some hopes that it might retest US$100,000 this year, although recent market tumult in part from concerns over spending on artificial intelligence has tempered expectations.

“Bitcoin has been incredibly resilient given macro shocks and AI trade unwind,” said Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at digital-asset hedge fund Apollo Crypto. “The next move is expected to be higher.”

title: Singapore dollar gains on yen as carry funder, analysts say
article:
(Oct 22): The Singapore dollar is gaining favour as a funding currency for carry trades as cheap borrowing costs and fading expectations for appreciation make it increasingly attractive relative to the Japanese yen, strategists said.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) kept policy settings unchanged last week in a surprise move, reinforcing expectations for more limited currency gains after tightening in April and July. At the same time, strong safe-haven inflows into Singapore have flooded local money markets, pushing down forward-implied yields, a measure of short-term borrowing costs.

That combination of cheap funding and low currency volatility is burnishing the Singapore dollar’s appeal for investors looking to borrow in one currency and buy higher-yielding assets elsewhere. It also offers an alternative to the yen, the traditional carry-trade funding currency, as Bank of Japan (BOJ) rate hikes raise borrowing costs and increase the risk of further currency appreciation.

“Funding in the Singapore dollar is attractive due to the negative carry, as Singapore’s foreign exchange implied yields are lower relative to most peers, and from limited upside for the currency,” said Abbas Keshvani, an Asian macro strategist at RBC Capital Markets. In comparison, the funding in the yen is at the risk of further policy normalisation from the BOJ, he added.

The divergence between the two central banks highlights the shift.

The BOJ raised policy rates by 25 basis points in September, with swap markets pricing an 80% probability of another quarter-point hike by December. A Bloomberg survey of economists showed 67% of respondents expect the BOJ to raise rates every three months, up from 46% in the last survey. That hawkish backdrop has supported a 3.3% gain in the yen against the greenback in the second half of the year, compared with a 1.3% rise in the Singapore dollar.

See also: Exporter dollar sales boost Malaysian ringgit, analysts say

Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar’s three-month forward-implied yield hovers around 1.65%, placing it among the cheapest funding currencies alongside the yen and Swiss franc in a group of 38 developed and emerging-market currencies, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The Singapore dollar has also become less volatile, reducing the risk that exchange-rate moves wipe out extra yield investors earn from a carry trade. Three-month option-implied volatility for the dollar-Singapore dollar pair has dropped to 3.55%, posting the biggest decline over the past year among Southeast Asian peers.

See also: Taiwan dollar, won slump as chip selloff hurts Asian currencies

“Singapore dollar rates are low compared to typical high-yielding currencies, so it can function as a carry funder,” said Dwyfor Evans, the head of Asia-Pacific macro strategy at State Street Markets.

The MAS decision may reinforce that appeal. The Singapore central bank uses the exchange rate as its main policy tool rather than interest rates. Its decision this month to leave the band’s slope unchanged marked a pause after consecutive rounds of tightening.

“We suspect the market will go back to seeing the Singapore dollar as a potential funding currency in the region,” HSBC Holdings plc strategist Joey Chew wrote in an Oct 14 note following the decision. “There has been downward pressure on the Singapore dollar, likely stemming from its low interest rates.”

title: Westpac axes 140 more roles as Australia bank job cuts intensify
article:
(Oct 22): Westpac Banking Corp is cutting another 140 roles, the latest sign that Australia’s weak housing market and an increased use of artificial intelligence technology are biting into the country’s workforce.

The Sydney-based bank informed the Finance Sector Union of 140 job cuts this week, following a further 102 cuts announced to the union two weeks ago, according to a Westpac spokesperson. The latest cuts will target roles across the bank, according to a Thursday statement from the FSU, with the earlier reductions impacting Westpac’s risk, institutional banking and finance teams, the union said.

Australia’s banking sector has seen a slew of headcount reductions as firms restructure. On Tuesday, National Australia Bank Ltd. announced up to 2,500 job cuts just over a year after ANZ Group Holdings Ltd said it would trim headcount by around 3,500. In May, Commonwealth Bank of Australia floated the prospect of job cuts as the bank increases its adoption of AI.

“The shape of our workforce changes according to the investment priorities of the Group,” a Westpac spokesperson said in a statement. Westpac has more than 30,000 staff. “As customer habits change, and the skills and capabilities required in banking continue to evolve, so will our workforce.”

Westpac seeks to retain staff where possible and offers support for those who depart, the spokesperson said. “While we continue to invest in extra bankers, digital delivery and customer-facing roles, other programs may be completing or require fewer resources.”

Australia’s jobless rate has ticked up to 4.7% in recent weeks as the Reserve Bank executes the most aggressive tightening cycle among developed economies this year.

See also: HDFC Bank probe finds that senior executives leaked secrets — Bloomberg

The layoffs bring the total number of job reductions to more than 10,000 for the banking sector in the past two years, according to FSU estimates.

“Although a range of macro-economic excuses have been offered by the banks, the FSU believes the seductive automation potential of AI is really driving their hunger for the emerging technology,” according to the union’s Thursday statement. “A lack of strong regulatory guardrails for AI is another factor adding to workers’ sense of vulnerability.”

Moves to reduce staff follow a slump in the housing market that has weakened home lending — traditionally an important source of earnings for Australian banks. Four interest rate increases from the country’s central bank has also added pressure on businesses and households, weakening sentiment.

See also: BHP cuts 300 workers at Australian iron ore mines as costs rise

Global peers are also trimming headcount. HSBC Holdings Plc is considering reducing up to 10% of its workforce, which would impact around 20,000 roles, while Standard Chartered Plc plans to eliminate around 8,000 support jobs over the next four years.

title: Chinese stocks set for bear market as tech sinks, policy hopes ebb
article:
(Oct 22): Chinese stocks entered a bear market, with US$2.4 trillion ($3.1 trillion) lost since a peak in May, as a protracted slump in consumption and mounting doubts over the profitability of artificial intelligence (AI) companies turn them into one of the world’s worst performers.

The CSI 300 Index closed 1.8% lower on Thursday, bringing its total losses from a high in June to 20%. Gauges for major Chinese companies and tech firms also plunged in Hong Kong, with a months-long sell-off showing little sign of abating.

The declines mark a sharp reversal from the stimulus-driven rally sparked in late 2024 that then gained momentum from AI bets before succumbing to a global sell-off in technology names. While policymakers have stepped up market supportive measures, the lack of a broad-based spending package and economic growth that’s barely meeting national targets have disappointed investors. Some analysts say the malaise may well extend into next year.

“This slide is too rapid and may just herald further declines ahead,” said Fu Zhifeng, the chief investment officer of Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management. “If there is no turnaround in market overhangs, including weak domestic demand, uncertainty over how to justify hefty AI spending and European and US government bond yields, investors are unlikely to change their trading strategies anytime soon.”

The rout in Chinese onshore shares has erased US$2.4 trillion in market value from a recent peak, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index and the CSI 300 gauge both rank among the worst performing major equity indexes globally this year, with losses of more than 10% each.

See also: Huawei gets US$2.3 bil offshore loan as chip spending soars — Bloomberg

Mixed results from US megacaps are also casting doubts on the durability of the AI rally as investors grow more discerning over valuations amid rising borrowing costs. In China, early optimism over technological breakthroughs and strong state support drove valuations to lofty levels, leaving the sector more vulnerable as sentiment turns.

The Hang Seng Tech Index slumped as much 5.3% on Thursday, the biggest intraday drop since July 17, as regulatory and business challenges facing China’s e-commerce industry weighed on tech giants including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. A gauge of major Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong dropped as much as 3.5%.

“Although Chinese tech trades at a significant discount to its global peers, weak earnings growth and potential earnings dilution mean the shares could stay rangebound or drift lower without a meaningful catalyst,” said Jeremy Tan, the chief executive officer of Tiger Fund Management in Singapore.

See also: PBOC faces multi-month road to new rate anchor, analysts say

Authorities have moved to curb selling pressure and stabilise its equity market, though analysts said state-backed buying alone may not be enough to enable a sustained recovery. Persistently weak sentiment may blunt the impact of the purchases.

A similar challenge emerged in 2024, when sustained buying through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) cushioned stocks through the summer, but failed to deliver a lasting turnaround until broader policy measures lifted sentiment in September.

Turnover in a basket of nine ETFs known to be traded by the national team reached 52 billion yuan (US$7.79 billion or $9.94 billion) as of 2.45pm local time, the most since the 62.8 billion yuan on Oct 15.

“With no global equities rebound to rely on, the national team might need to buy more and do so for longer than in its two most recent rescues, during the April 2025 tariff shock and the July 2026 technology sell-off,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts including Rebecca Sin wrote in a note.

The outstanding amount of margin trades — or bets funded by borrowed cash — has dropped to a level last seen in late 2025, underscoring waning risk appetite. The daily turnover in China’s onshore stocks has been hovering around the lowest level in about 15 months.

“Investor sentiment remains very poor for China’s onshore and offshore markets, and without new policy or tech catalysts, this kind of volatile, directionless environment may persist into early 2027,” said Homin Lee, a senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore.

title: Tesla’s lowered capex target fuels doubt on AI, robotics goals
article:
(Oct 22): Tesla Inc pulled back its spending plans after investment last quarter trailed expectations, clouding Elon Musk’s effort to transform the electric vehicle (EV) maker into an artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics company.

Capital expenditures (capex) will be around US$20 billion ($25.5 billion) this year, the company said on Wednesday after reporting earnings results. That marked a reversal from earlier this year, when Tesla raised the target to more than US$25 billion.

Tesla had been consistently short of the pace needed to hit its spending goal, particularly after a US$4.73 billion outlay in the third quarter. Analysts had expected US$7.95 billion on average in estimates compiled by Bloomberg.

Heavy spending is needed to help Tesla reorient its operations around futuristic business lines such as AI, robots and autonomous driving. The shift is seen as a central justification for a potential merger with SpaceX — a historic transaction that Musk this week said the companies are exploring.

“For almost any company, spending less and generating cash is good news. Tesla is the exception because the stock is not priced as a car company,” said Dave Mazza, the chief executive officer of Roundhill Investments. “Capex is the only hard number investors have for how fast Optimus and Cybercab are actually being built, and cutting the guide by US$5 billion six months after raising it by US$5 billion looks less like discipline and more like the ramp slipping for the future.”

The capex figure was a notable surprise in a quarter that also saw Tesla beat analysts’ profit estimates. Adjusted earnings were 48 cents a share in the period, while Wall Street had anticipated 44 cents on average. Revenue of US$28.05 billion was slightly below expectations.

See also: Intel touts factory expansion progress in sign of growing demand

The shares had fallen 3.5% at 7.23pm in extended trading in New York. Tesla stock fell 14% this year through Wednesday’s close.

The company’s initiatives are currently supported by a narrow product line-up that consists of only three vehicles: the Y and 3 models, along with the polarising Cybertruck. Competition for EVs is also heating up. Tesla ended the quarter with the largest passenger vehicle backlog in four years, citing battery availability as a limiting factor. The company has lined up US$30 billion of new loans and credit lines to underpin its growth.

See also: IBM posts 5% sales growth, says infrastructure deals came back

On the company’s call with analysts on Wednesday, chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said capital expenditures will continue to grow as Tesla invests in its robotaxi fleet and expands production for the humanoid robot Optimus and solar products. It’s also spending on improving computing infrastructure and building a semiconductor plant.

Musk tempered expectations around the timeline for Optimus, citing supply-chain challenges and design changes, the need for more training data and continued difficulties with the hand design. It will likely take until the end of 2027 for Tesla to work through the various issues, he said.

“Lower capex is only a positive if it doesn’t come at the expense of future growth,” said Haris Khurshid, the chief investment officer of Karobaar Capital. “Given how much their future valuation depends on robotaxi and Optimus, I want to know whether the spending is simply shifting between quarters or whether the ramp is taking longer than expected.”

Musk declined to offer more details of whether Tesla could combine with SpaceX.

On SpaceX’s investor call a day earlier, he confirmed that both companies have formed special committees to explore a possible merger, but said no agreement has been reached. Musk said he’s not allowed to participate in talks but supports a deal, while warning that it may not materialise. He cited the challenge of getting enough support from Tesla shareholders.

Tesla said over 75% of new deliveries in North America during the quarter included subscriptions to the company’s driver-assistant software, called FSD Supervised in the US. The EV maker also got approval for the software in four more European countries during the quarter.

Last month, Tesla opened its first factory for its long-awaited Semi freight truck — a product that was first unveiled in 2017.

Earlier this month, Tesla posted stronger-than-expected vehicle sales for the third quarter. It held an event to unveil its Roadster vehicle last week, including a demonstration in collaboration with SpaceX that showed a flying version of the vehicle performing aerial stunts. The niche product isn’t expected to significantly impact the company’s performance.

The EV maker also launched its two-seater Cybercab in September and has been integrating the autonomous car into its Austin robotaxi fleet. The event drew scrutiny from US regulators at the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

Tesla expanded its robotaxi fleet size and hours during the quarter, but hasn’t added new cities since July. The company has a goal of adding service in Las Vegas and Phoenix.

In a post earlier on Wednesday, Tesla said its robotaxi service would expand “soon” to Phoenix, Las Vegas, Jacksonville, Florida, and San Antonio, Texas, without giving a concrete timeline.

In September, Tesla cleared one of its last regulatory hurdles in Arizona to start the service in the state. Separately, it was approved to operate a fleet of up to 5,000 autonomous vehicles in parts of Clark County, where Las Vegas is located.

Tesla expects to launch Cybercab in Dallas next month, with plans to scale to other cities from there. Executives said the company could sell a small amount of Cybercabs to customers by the end of the year, but added the vehicle will primarily be owned by Tesla and used as a transportation service.

title: A Tesla-SpaceX merger may boost Musk’s fortune by US$110 bil
article:
(Oct 22): Elon Musk made headlines on SpaceX’s earnings call when he confirmed that it and Tesla Inc had formed special committees to explore a potential merger.

“We are pretty much in the super-intelligence singularity,” said Musk. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating.”

Depending on the details of a merger, there could also be a lot to gain for Musk.

A tie-up could add more than US$110 billion ($140 billion) to his fortune by accelerating the vesting of Tesla shares that otherwise wouldn’t vest until 2028, according to calculations by the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. And depending on Tesla’s valuation in a deal, it could unlock billions more from Musk’s 2025 compensation package without Tesla having to meet the operating milestones that would otherwise be required to trigger the payout.

Tesla and SpaceX didn’t reply to requests for comments. Musk’s fortune soared by more than US$60 billion on Wednesday after shares of both companies rose on news of the merger discussions and strong quarterly earnings from SpaceX.

See also: Taiwan rejects Grab’s US$600 mil takeover of Foodpanda unit

Musk, 55, was handed a record-breaking pay package at Tesla last year that could be worth nearly US$1 trillion if fully earned. Spanning 10 years, it’s subject to ambitious performance goals including delivering a million Optimus robots, having a million robotaxis in commercial operation and delivering 20 million vehicles.

It paired the goals with market capitalisation targets of between US$2 trillion and US$8.5 trillion. All of the operational and market-cap milestones have yet to be achieved.

Like most executive compensation plans, Musk’s is subject to change-in-control provisions. A merger can trigger them if Tesla’s existing shareholders emerge with less than 50% of the voting power of the surviving company or its parent. That would be a plausible outcome given SpaceX is currently worth roughly one-third more than Tesla, but would ultimately depend on the transaction’s structure.

See also: SpaceX, Tesla boards to study potential US$3.5 tril merger

If the provisions are triggered, then the operational milestones are disregarded and Musk’s payout is calculated using Tesla’s market value in the deal.

That means that if Tesla is valued at US$2 trillion in the merger — the first market-cap milestone — Musk would unlock shares with a net value of more than US$6 billion. Tesla is currently worth about US$1.5 trillion.

“Whether these change-in-control provisions technically trigger will depend on how the deal is structured, but shareholders on both sides should assume his incentives point towards a high headline valuation and ask what the committees will do about it,” said Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor of accounting at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business.

Under the current package, Musk can’t sell the shares from the award for five years, but that’s also subject to exceptions for change-in-control events.

An even bigger benefit for Musk could come from the accelerated vesting of his 2018 Tesla compensation award.

Tesla's signage on an options contract ticker on the floor of the American Stock Exchange at the New York Stock Exchange.

Musk’s original “moonshot” pay package gave him about 304 million options subject to Tesla meeting certain market-cap and operational milestones, all of which were accomplished. Musk and the board negotiated an implementation package earlier this year that allowed him to net-settle the options, reducing his need for cash to pay taxes and exercise costs. In return, the roughly 286 million shares he received won’t vest until January 2028 as an added incentive for him to stay at the company.

But if there’s a change-in-control, those shares vest immediately.

Additionally, after vesting, those shares are subject to a five-year holding period. But the agreement provides for some exceptions in a change-of-control event, potentially allowing Musk to sell them earlier too.

The shares are currently worth more than US$110 billion, and are excluded from Musk’s current net worth calculation on Bloomberg’s wealth index because they haven’t yet vested.

Musk also has two compensation packages at SpaceX that are less likely to be affected by any deal.

The rocket and artificial intelligence (AI) company awarded him up to 1.3 billion restricted shares dependent on market capitalisation milestones as well as operational milestones tied to a human colony on Mars and the computing power of its planned space-based data centres.

The market-cap milestones can be adjusted by the board to account for any mergers or acquisitions, which it did after SpaceX bought Musk’s AI start-up, xAI. That suggests the board would again adjust them in the event of a Tesla merger, so that the deal doesn’t make achieving those goals artificially easier.

But there could be pressure on the board to craft another compensation package for its founder, given the forfeiture of most of his Tesla compensation package and the lack of explicit goals for Musk that would be tied to Tesla’s traditional business lines.

That “would seem a foregone conclusion, given the history of both companies in granting very large equity packages”, said Schloetzer. “The combined company’s board would face the familiar argument that new awards are needed to keep Musk engaged.”

title: AI trade stumbles after tech earnings; oil gains
article:
(Oct 22): Stocks fell on Thursday as megacap earnings failed to reassure investors about the rebound in the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, Chinese equities neared a bear market and escalating Middle East tensions drove oil prices higher.

Contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index slipped 1.3% and those for the S&P 500 dropped 0.7%, as a split set of results from Tesla Inc and Meta Platforms Inc raised doubts about the recent rebound in AI stocks.

In Asia, the Kospi Index — a barometer for the AI trade — declined over 3% as chip heavyweights Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc retreated. China’s CSI 300 Index fell 1.3% and was set for a bear market. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd led Chinese e-commerce shares lower after the government called for quality control. The broader MSCI Asia-Pacific Index lost 1.6%, set for its lowest close since end-July.

Tesla shares dropped 3.3% in post-market trading after cutting its capital-spending forecast. Meta Platforms, however, rose 2.2% after hours as the company boosted its bet on AI with spending outlook. Shares of the semiconductor capital equipment company Lam Research Corp fell 7.4% in extended trading after a weaker-than-expected earnings forecast.

“The market is a hard one to please on capital expenditure right now,” said Tim Waterer, the chief market analyst of KCM Trade. “It frets when companies ramp spending, and it frets when they pull it back, as we have just seen with Tesla. In this environment, it’s almost impossible to get the balance right.”

Adding to the pressure, crude oil advanced after deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns that escalating Middle East hostilities could hit supply. Brent climbed 1.7% to trade around US$110.70 a barrel. Treasuries rose on haven demand, while bitcoin and gold declined.

See also: In search of blue skies

The latest corporate results will test whether earnings can keep the AI trade on track as investors weigh strong growth against the mounting cost of funding the industry’s expansion. Concerns have grown that heavy spending on data centres and computing capacity may take longer to generate returns, while this year’s blistering stock rally has raised questions about stretched valuations and the risk of an AI bubble.

“Markets are basically telling us we are moving on from trading AI vibes and narrative to now requiring a pretty high bar for what an earnings beat looks like,” Kaanhari Singh, the Asia-Pacific head of equity derivatives sales at Barclays plc, said on Bloomberg TV. “That’s both in terms of capex forward guidance, but also for the path of monetisation.”

In other corners of the market, Treasuries climbed across the curve on Thursday, pushing long-end yields to the lowest in a month, as renewed doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade drove investors towards havens.

See also: Asian stocks advance as chip sell-off eases

The 30-year yield dropped three basis points to 5.38%, its lowest since Sept 23.

A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar’s strength slipped 0.1%. Gold declined 1.2% to extend its losses this week and trade around US$4,100 an ounce.

Bitcoin fell over 2% to about US$82,800, leading cryptocurrencies lower.

Doubts over the economics of the AI boom have rattled markets recently, with shareholders demanding clearer evidence that enormous outlays on infrastructure will eventually pay off.

The repricing has been sharp. The Nasdaq 100 lost 5.5% last week, its steepest weekly decline since US President Donald Trump unveiled global tariffs in April 2025. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slid for eight consecutive sessions, marking its longest run of losses since October 2008.

Attention is also on the rising tensions in the Middle East and the oil market.

The US State Department issued an ordered departure for non-emergency personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia because of the growing threat from Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen.

The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

Investors aren’t “comfortable with oil rising above 110”, said Rajeev De Mello, a global macro portfolio manager at Gama Asset Management. “We are regularly making new highs in oil and energy products, which is stagflationary. Implied volatility on oil options is rising once again reflecting uncertainty about the future path of energy as we approach the Northern Hemisphere winter.”

• Texas Instruments Inc, the biggest maker of analog and embedded processing chips, gave a strong revenue forecast for the current period, lifted by demand from automotive and industrial customers.
