title: Barclays’ Middle East expansion plans ‘on track,’ Khanna says
article:
(Oct 22): Barclays Plc is continuing with plans to expand in Saudi Arabia and the wider Middle East, keeping its “constructive” view on the region, according to the bank’s Asia-Pacific chief executive officer Jaideep Khanna.

“We are a big believer” in the opportunity in the Middle East, Khanna said Thursday in a Bloomberg TV interview in Singapore, where the London-based firm hosted the Barclays Asia Forum. “We are growing and investing in our aggregate Middle East presence.”

The bank is seeking a financial services licence to establish a full-fledged platform in Saudi Arabia and looking to build out in Türkiye as well, said Khanna, who also has some oversight into the region.

His comments affirm plans by CEO CS Venkatakrishnan, who said in April that the bank was pushing ahead in Saudi Arabia, where Barclays aims to open a regional headquarters later this year despite the war. Since then, the Middle East conflict has continued to deteriorate, with Riyadh suffering deadly strikes from Iran-backed militants. The kingdom this week postponed its flagship conference, the Future Investment Initiative, to next year because of the attacks. Venkatakrishnan was on the list of high-profile speakers that also included the CEOs from JPMorgan Chase & Co and HSBC Holdings Plc.

Elsewhere, Barclays is optimistic on Asia, where it counts Japan and India among key markets. The region is becoming “a lot more significant’ particularly to the dealmaking business, according to Khanna. He also said China remains an important opportunity that no global investment bank can ignore.

In Japan, where the firm just returned to the high-touch cash equities business, Khanna said it is a market of “particular interest” given the greater attention from fixed income investors and fund inflows to the stock market. The bank is prepared to pay for talent given the competition, and is focused on strengthening the existing platform rather than go into new areas, he added.

See also: Citi targets top spot in China as it awaits securities licence

title: Intel touts factory expansion progress in sign of growing demand
article:
(Oct 22): Intel Corp touted progress with its long-delayed US factory expansion, saying it is finishing up a plant in Arizona and making headway on the chipmaker’s newest site in Ohio.

Tool installation — a key final step — is underway at the Fab 62 plant near Phoenix, Intel Vice President Naga Chandrasekaran said in a post on the company’s website. In New Albany, Ohio, meanwhile, Intel has installed the first major roof truss.

Intel is betting that the new factories can help restore the company’s leadership in the chip industry and hone its technological edge. The Silicon Valley pioneer is also in the early stages of becoming a semiconductor foundry, a role in which it produces chips for outside clients.

The company has grown more cautious about overspending under chief executive officer Lip-Bu Tan. The CEO, who took the helm in March 2025, has said that projects such as the Ohio facility will only go ahead when he’s sure there’s enough work for them. That suggests the chipmaker is now growing more confident about having demand for the new plants.

Intel has been developing two new facilities near Phoenix, located in the company’s Ocotillo Campus south of the city. Fab 52 is already operational, and Fab 62 is poised to open next door. It also has factories in the area devoted to less-advanced production.

Filling chip plants with the machinery that produces the electronic components is by far the most expensive stage of getting them ready for manufacturing. Individual tools can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. The Fab 62 facility will be in operation at the beginning of 2028, Intel said.

See also: IBM posts 5% sales growth, says infrastructure deals came back

Under Tan’s predecessor, Pat Gelsinger, Intel positioned itself as central to attempts to restore cutting-edge chip production to the US. But that effort was undermined by the company’s loss of leadership in chip manufacturing technology over the last decade. Intel also struggled to lure enough foundry customers to justify its investments. That left its expansion plans languishing for years.

The Ohio site was envisioned as the largest chipmaking facility in the world and a symbol of Intel’s resurgence. After some initial construction and public fanfare — including a visit by former US president Joe Biden in 2022 — work went on hiatus. Intel’s announcement on Wednesday shows that the effort is moving forward again.

Historically, chip companies often build factory shells — the outer structure — and then wait to purchase and install equipment until demand is solid. Though Intel has yet to announce many high-profile foundry customers, it’s currently seeing a surge in orders for its own products — specifically data centre processors used to run AI services — and is struggling to keep up.

See also: DeepSeek raises US$15 bil in challenge to leading US labs — Bloomberg

In July, the company said it would spend more than previously forecast on new plants and equipment, with the budget reaching about $20 billion this year. In 2027, it expects that number to go up significantly.

Even with that renewed optimism, it’s still not investing as much as industry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), which Wall Street projects will spend roughly US$60 billion ($76.6 billion). South Korea’s Samsung Electronics Co, another chip foundry, is also significantly outspending the US company.

title: IBM posts 5% sales growth, says infrastructure deals came back
article:
(Oct 22): International Business Machines Corp (IBM) reported sales that topped analysts’ estimates, saying it had recovered most of the infrastructure deals that were delayed earlier this year.

Sales increased about 5% to US$17.1 billion ($21.8 billion) in the quarter ended Sept 30, the company said on Wednesday in a statement. IBM’s infrastructure unit, which includes mainframe servers, expanded 4% to US$3.7 billion. Both were ahead of analysts’ average projections, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

About two-thirds of the mainframe and associated software deals that slipped earlier this year have since been inked, chief financial officer Jim Kavanaugh said in an interview.

In July, IBM said that customers were temporarily shifting their spending to chips and servers amid artificial intelligence (AI)-fuelled shortages, harming its mainframe and software units. This fuelled panic among investors already concerned that AI tools will disrupt many software incumbents and sent the shares down 25%, the worst day since at least 1968.

IBM’s closely watched software unit expanded 8.3% to US$7.8 billion, ahead of the US$7.64 billion anticipated by Wall Street. Big Blue has sought to refashion itself as a high-growth software company through major acquisitions of Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent.

For the full year, the company now expects free cash flow to increase by more than US$1 billion. Previously, it expected about US$1 billion. Profit, excluding some items, was US$2.95 a share in the third quarter, compared with the average estimate of US$2.86.

See also: DeepSeek raises US$15 bil in challenge to leading US labs — Bloomberg

The shares gained about 5% in extended trading after closing at US$251.46 in New York. The stock declined 15% this year through Wednesday’s close.

title: DeepSeek raises US$15 bil in challenge to leading US labs — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 22): The Chinese AI pioneer DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan (US$15 billion) in its latest fundraising round, one of the country’s largest ever and a sign of the startup’s ambitions to compete globally with the likes of Anthropic PBC and OpenAI.

The Hangzhou-based firm boosted its financing target at least twice as it talked with investors, from 50 billion yuan to 80 billion yuan before reaching the final tally, according to people familiar with the matter. Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL) and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings Ltd were among the biggest investors in the round, said the people, asking not to be named as the details aren’t public.

DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. The AI upstart triggered a US$1 trillion meltdown in global markets in 2025 when it showed the ability to compete with Silicon Valley’s leaders at a fraction of the cost of their models, but it’s never had the financial resources of the US frontier labs.

The latest fundraising shows that imbalance is beginning to moderate, although it still has far less financial firepower than Anthropic and OpenAI, which have each raised more than US$100 billion. Like rival Moonshot, DeepSeek is preparing for an initial public offering that would be an important milestone for Chinese markets, Bloomberg News has reported.

DeepSeek has begun to spend more aggressively to build out AI data centres and to develop more open-source models for use in China and abroad.

The firm has regularly rolled out high-performance, low-cost models that put pressure on its domestic competitors and gained customers in the US and other overseas markets. In September, for example, it dropped V4.1 Flash, setting off a drop in the share prices of local rivals MiniMax Group Inc and Z.AI Co. DeepSeek, Tencent and CATL representatives didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.

See also: Super Micro jumps after positive preliminary results top estimates

More broadly, companies from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd to ByteDance Ltd have introduced low-cost AI services, typically open-sourced so customers can modify them as needed.

One widely shared benchmark chart from Artificial Analysis sketched out what has been called the “DeepSeek death zone,” where competitors will struggle to survive if they can’t beat the firm’s performance or they can’t charge lower prices.

title: Meta touts AI progress while escalating its bet on the market
article:
(Oct 22): Meta Platforms Inc chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg told investors that a pricey wager on artificial intelligence (AI) is delivering results, setting the stage for the company to bet even more aggressively on the market.

During its quarterly earnings report on Wednesday, the social-media giant boosted its capital spending plans for the year and announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses.

The moves show that Meta has confidence that its already-stratospheric spending on AI is bearing fruit. After struggling to persuade investors to accept ballooning costs, Meta has made headway with its technology in recent months, especially with a new AI agent called Muse. Zuckerberg pointed to that progress as reason to keep ploughing ahead.

“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we are seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in Wednesday’s report.

Meta shares rose more than 2% in after-hours trading on Wednesday. They had gained about 6% this year through the close in New York.

The results kicked off a technology earnings season that’s likely to focus on runaway AI expenditures — and attempts by companies to get a return on investment. Google parent Alphabet Inc, Microsoft Corp and Amazon.com Inc, three of the other biggest spenders on AI data centres, are slated to deliver their quarterly results next week.

See also: AI to spur Southeast Asian digital economy to US$368 bil, study shows

At Meta, capital expenditures will be US$135 billion ($172 billion) to US$145 billion in 2026, the Menlo Park, California-based company said, raising the bottom end of the range from US$130 billion.

The new class of shares will be distributed to existing investors through a stock dividend. Holders will get one share of the new stock in what will essentially be a two-for-one stock split, Meta said. It expects trading of the new shares to begin in January.

The stock will also be a tool to help further Meta’s expansion. It will be used for capital fundraising, employee compensation and potential takeovers, Meta said.

See also: Anthropic may spend US$750 bil in coming years, report says

This isn’t the first time the company — formerly Facebook Inc — has attempted such a plan. In 2017, it scrapped an unpopular effort to create a class of shares that would have helped Zuckerberg retain voting control of the business he co-founded. At the time, Facebook had a valuation of roughly US$500 billion. Today, Meta’s market capitalisation stands at nearly US$1.8 trillion.

In announcing the new stock class, Meta said the non-voting shares would ensure that Zuckerberg continues to lead the company “into the next era”.

Zuckerberg touted the success of Muse during a conference call with analysts, saying that more than 10 million people have used the service in the US and Canada over its first six weeks.

“Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg said.

As part of the report, Meta said fourth-quarter revenue would be US$73 billion to US$76 billion. Analysts had estimated US$73.6 billion on average, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Third-quarter revenue rose 26% to US$64.6 billion, topping the US$63.3 billion estimate. Earnings amounted to US$3.83 a share in the period, beating the US$3.57 projection.

Over the last year and a half, Zuckerberg has refocused the company’s efforts on advancing in the AI race. The push has included committing hundreds of billions of dollars to build out the infrastructure needed to support its models and overhauling its AI unit under head Alexandr Wang.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Earlier this month, Meta launched Muse Wonder, a long-awaited new AI model with “frontier capabilities” that its leadership said put it on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude when it comes to coding or working through financial or legal questions. If Meta’s claims hold up to outside testing, and Muse Wonder gains traction with researchers and developers, it would mark a significant turnaround for the company, whose models last year fell flat in Silicon Valley.

The Muse personalised AI assistant debuted in September. It’s designed to automate a range of tasks for consumers, including shopping, buying movie tickets and scheduling appointments. Muse quickly rose to the top of mobile app charts.

But that success has come with a cost. Meta noted that the AI agent requires a great deal of computing power. That’s one of the reasons the company hasn’t launched the agent globally yet.

Zuckerberg said that Muse should remain free for most people, with Meta making money through transaction fees paid by businesses, subscriptions for heavy users and customers who want access to the most advanced models, and paid tools for companies that rely on Muse at work. “If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years,” he added.

Meta, the owner of Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, generates most of its current revenue from advertising.

Zuckerberg also said that CJ Desai will lead Meta’s new enterprise platform, the business the company is building to sell access to its models and AI services. Bloomberg News first reported on this emerging cloud business.

Meta still has a lot of spending left to do before the end of the year. Even though the midpoint of its capital expenditures outlook is US$140 billion, the company has only spent about US$86 billion through the first nine months.

Meta also signalled that it will take longer to see returns from some of its newer AI investments, even as its core business helps absorb the cost.

“While these investments will take longer to generate returns than those in our core business,” chief financial officer Susan Li said, “the breadth of monetisation opportunities and internal efficiencies gives us confidence in their long-term potential.”

Meta is cutting costs elsewhere as it bulldozes money into AI. Headcount was down 15% year over year following significant job cuts, and the company has pledged to narrow losses at Reality Labs, its hardware division.

Meta expects Reality Labs losses of as much as US$19 billion this year, before falling to around US$15 billion in 2027 as it reallocates spending towards other priorities — “primarily AI”.

title: Citi targets top spot in China as it awaits securities licence
article:
(Oct 22): Citigroup Inc is counting on securing an onshore securities licence in China as the US lender expands operations in the world’s second-largest economy following a string of major consumer exits across Asia.

“We’re hoping for it,” Ernesto Cantu, head of international at the New York-based bank, said in an interview, referring to the licence. “It’s important for us because right now we cannot do anything related to investment banking in the mainland.”

Citigroup harbours big ambitions to expand in the region, targeting the top spot among global investment banks in China, according to Cantu.

Progress has been slow, however, leaving the lender waiting almost five years for regulatory approvals. The delay stems from complications surrounding changing Chinese data-security regulations as well as heightened regulatory scrutiny in the US.

Despite these hurdles, mainland China remains Citigroup’s second-largest international market after the UK, boosted by the bank’s corporate client reach. Cantu, who visited the mainland in March, plans to return in November.

Asia remains “an important focus” for Citigroup as it deploys capital across the region, including in China and India, Cantu said. “A lot of Chinese companies are going global and we are helping them. India is also growing at a good pace.”

See also: EU nears market securitisation reform in bid to unleash billions

The bank is entering the final stretch of a sweeping global restructuring under chief executive officer Jane Fraser aimed at streamlining its footprint. To sharpen focus on its corporate and institutional business, the Wall Street firm shed its retail banking operations across 13 markets, including mainland China, India, and Indonesia.

That pivot is yielding results, according to Cantu, a three-decade company veteran who said that exit plans are “mostly done.”

“In some markets, overall revenues have grown significantly despite the sale of the consumer businesses,” he said.

See also: Starbucks China will require purchases to sit in its cafes

In India, after selling the consumer business in March 2023, Citigroup nearly doubled revenue and grew net income by 56%, while in Indonesia, excluding a one-time divestment premium in 2023, net income grew about 56% from 2023 to 2025, according to the bank.

Citi posted the best third quarter in a decade, boosted by trading and services business. Late last year, it traded above its book value for the first time since 2018 — a boost to Fraser’s turnaround plan.

The lender is now pushing ahead with an IPO for Mexico’s Grupo Financiero Banamex, having offloaded an additional 24% stake to investors, including Blackstone Inc. Citigroup still has a 51% stake in Banamex and plans to sell a small stake before the IPO next year, according to Cantu.

“There is investor demand for an incremental stake, which means it can be done quickly,” said Cantu. “We are talking to investors, including those that participated in the previous placement.”

The bank would likely sell a portion of its remaining stake through the IPO, with the rest sold in subsequent follow-on offerings, according to Cantu. He declined to say how much the bank is planning to raise.

Bloomberg has previously reported that Citigroup is targeting to raise more than US$3 billion for its initial public offering.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“We want to do the Banamex IPO in the first half, if the market is there,” said Cantu.

Going to IPO with a de-consolidated entity is a “better equity story” because that means that the governance of Banamex will be entirely in Banamex, he added.

Cantu, who was previously CEO of Citibanamex, said that an independent Banamex will be able to take on more risk, in line with the broader industry, and a sale is the “best decision” for Banamex.

In the Middle East, the lender has no plans to pare its exposure despite the ongoing turmoil, according to the banker.

Saudi Arabia this month suffered its deadliest strikes since the Iran war began as Houthi militants repeatedly targeted airports across the kingdom, prompting airlines to halt flights and the postponement of the kingdom’s flagship investment event.

Citigroup has business in other places including Ukraine, where it continues to do business despite the Russian invasion.

“We continue to believe that the Middle East as a consequence of this in many ways is going to come out stronger,” said Cantu. “If anything, the resiliency plans that they are implementing is going to make them stronger.”

title: EU nears market securitisation reform in bid to unleash billions
article:
(Oct 22): The European Union (EU) reached a provisional agreement to overhaul rules governing the bloc’s securitisations markets, a deal that would unleash billions of euros to finance initiatives in key areas such as defence and climate resilience.

Policymakers reached a political-level compromise to push ahead a plan that would allow banks to free up more capital to lend to households, firms and infrastructure projects. The framework would reduce banks’ capital requirements for low-risk deals and reduce administrative burden for market participants. The framework still needs to be finalised and formally endorsed.

“Securitisation plays a vital role in our financial eco-system by freeing up capital and supporting lending,” a representative for the Irish government, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, said in a statement. “Our objective here is simple: support market revival without compromising financial stability, investor protection or market integrity.”

The initiative is part of the EU’s savings and investment union, a package of reforms that aims to channel financial assets more efficiently and spur growth by funding key industries. The 27-country bloc is going ahead with reforms to the securitisation markets at a time when geopolitical uncertainty, high energy prices, government deficits and worries over the debt-fuelled AI boom are pushing up risk premiums across credit markets.

Europe had a total of €1.295 trillion (US$1.45 trillion) of securitisations outstanding, including collateralised loan obligations, at the end of March, according to the Association for Financial Markets in Europe. While that figure had grown 6.3% in a year, it is still a fraction of the US securitisation market.

Boosting the securitisation market is part of measures outlined by former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi to increase the bloc’s economic competitiveness. The review of the securitisation rules started in 2024.

See also: Starbucks China will require purchases to sit in its cafes

title: Bank of Singapore augments CIO with new sustainability advisory team
article:
To better support its clients and in particular, the ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) segment, the Bank of Singapore (BOS), the private banking subsidiary of OCBC, has established a dedicated sustainability advisory team under its chief investment office (CIO).

Led by Christine Cheong, the new sustainability partners team will work alongside relationship managers and subject matter experts from across the OCBC group to support clients across three interconnected dimensions — investments, businesses and multi-generational stewardship. Prior to assuming this role, she was responsible for formulating in-house ESG methodologies and ESG fund selection within the CIO.

“For many ultra-high-net-worth clients, sustainability has evolved from an investment consideration into a broader question of stewardship,” says Cheong. “Our role is to help them navigate those connections and make informed decisions aligned with their long-term priorities.”

According to BOS, UHNW clients are often entrepreneurs and business owners who are seeking guidance not only on sustainability-related investment opportunities, but also on navigating the sustainability transition within their own businesses and creating lasting impact across generations.

Jean Chia, BOS global chief investment officer, says: “As clients' wealth and business interests become increasingly interconnected, they seek advice that spans both domains. The sustainability partners team strengthens our ability to harness sustainability expertise from across the OCBC group, supporting clients not only in their investment portfolios, but also across their businesses, family interests and broader community ambitions as they navigate the transition to a more sustainable future.”

Over the past year, BOS has strengthened its family office and wealth advisory senior bench to support its UHNW push.

title: Malaysia allows first export of raw rare earths under new rules
article:
(Oct 22): Malaysia has given the go-ahead for a batch of unprocessed rare earths to be exported, the first approval under a new framework designed to permit testing and potentially encourage investments in local capacity.

A single export application for research and development purposes has been permitted by the Department of Mineral and Geoscience Malaysia, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability said in response to a Bloomberg query. It did not identify the applicant or provide details.

Rare earths are among the most critical raw materials on the planet, deeply embedded in the technologies that underpin modern life, including an array of key defence applications. While China has long dominated their mining and processing, other nations including Malaysia are now stepping up efforts to develop their own capacity in a push to reduce reliance on Beijing.

At present, the Southeast Asian nation hosts Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths Ltd, one of only two major producers outside China, with local conglomerates including Berjaya Corp Bhd (KL:BJCORP) also exploring projects. Among other overseas companies, France’s Carester SAS plans to build a rare-earths separation plant ​in the northern state of Perak with Malaysia’s ‌Malaco Mining Group, and more than a dozen US firms are also exploring local opportunities.

Earlier this month, Malaysia released guidelines for the conditional export of raw rare earths, easing a moratorium that had been in place since 2024. Under the revised framework, shipments of unprocessed materials can be permitted for research and development or processing, subject to conditions.

“The guidelines are open to eligible applicants, including foreign companies, subject to compliance with the relevant regulatory requirements,” the ministry said. The priority is not the number of applications approved, but quality of investments, technology transfer and long-term value creation, it added.

See also: Malaysia's September exports surge to five-year high on AI demand

title: Oil rises as deadly Saudi attack fans Middle East supply fears
article:
(Oct 22) : Oil rose following a deadly attack on a Saudi oil field, raising concerns that escalating hostilities in the Middle East could hit supply even as exports through the Strait of Hormuz have accelerated in recent months.

West Texas Intermediate climbed toward US$98 a barrel after swinging in a US$4 range Wednesday. Brent jumped above US$110 in post-settlement trading. A drone strike on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah field killed two people, although operations were unaffected. Meanwhile, the US has ordered the departure of some personnel and family members from American embassies in the kingdom.

Global benchmark Brent has surged almost 80% this year after the US-Iran war disrupted energy flows from the Persian Gulf. Still, exports have increased recently as tankers have switched off their transponders to avoid detection. Shipments of crude have returned close to prewar levels, according to estimates from traders and banks, although oil-product flows remain constrained.

The squeeze has been more acute in refined products, most notably diesel, and has been compounded by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Governments are tapping stockpiles to ease tightness, while US President Donald Trump is pushing measures to lower energy prices ahead of next month’s midterm elections, including Russia-related tariff waivers, a diesel deal with Moscow and the sale of sanctioned tankers.

Separately, US crude inventories dropped by just over 3 million barrels, with another 300,000 barrels withdrawn from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, according to the Energy Information Administration. Distillate inventories rose by almost 2 million barrels, offering some relief to diesel and heating oil markets strained by tight supplies and elevated prices.

title: Stocks climb in late hours on Meta’s big AI wagers
article:
(Oct 22) : Wall Street’s wagers on artificial intelligence regained traction, with stocks rising in late hours as solid results bolstered confidence in the trade that has powered the bull market.

An exchange-traded fund tracking the S&P 500 rose after the close of regular trading. Tesla Inc.’s profit beat estimates, assuaging worries about increased investments into new areas such as AI. Meta Platforms Inc. boosted its capital spending outlook and announced plans to create a new class of nonvoting stock, part of efforts to escalate its bet on technology.

“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Meta’s Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said in Wednesday’s report.

In regular hours, tech shares powered gains as a blowout earnings report from SpaceX eased concern over whether the AI investment boom can prove sustainable. Super Micro Computer Inc. jumped on solid preliminary figures. The Nasdaq 100 rose 1.1%.

Investors’ anxiety over the durability of the AI trade had recently surged amid fears that the substantial upfront capital spending the technology needs will take longer than expected to translate into profits and productivity gains.

“So, does this signal that the worst is over when it comes to the selloff across tech, and in particular chip stocks, seen since the beginning of this month? Maybe,” said David Morrison at Trade Nation. “Certainly, there has been yet another impressive start to the earnings season.”

See also: US stock futures advance on AI earnings boost

“Despite hedge funds sharply reducing tech exposure, the market isn’t giving up on AI,” said Mark Hackett at Nationwide. “Investors simply want to see the payoff, and SpaceX earnings may be an early sign of that.”

Billionaire Ken Griffin said investors are “almost certainly” in the midst of an AI bubble as many companies are still grappling with just how much they’ll spend on the technology and how it will transform the economy.

BlackRock Inc. Chief Executive Officer Larry Fink warned that delays in building data centers could raise computing costs and threaten economic growth as demand for AI accelerates.

See also: Oil steadies as traders weigh conflicting signals on Iran talks

“If we don’t build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now,” Fink said in an interview on Bloomberg Television Wednesday, on the sidelines of the Berlin Global Dialogue event. “And the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost.”

Elsewhere, oil whipsawed after its settlement. The US State Department issued an ordered departure for non-emergency personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia because of the growing threat from Houthi militants in neighboring Yemen.
